correctness.rationale: The standard-library code exhaustively builds each permitted word for n=1,...,9, defines deletion shadows by all possible single deletions, and searches every compatible clique with a sound greedy proper-coloring pruning bound. It verifies the complete optimum vector (1,2,2,3,3,6,6,10,13), a thirteen-word witness, and all ten VT residue counts at n=9 (11,10,12,12,10,11,10,12,12,10). An independent incidence-MILP implementation confirms n=7,8,9, without serving as proof. Finite enumeration is exhaustive for the explicitly finite domain, not a claim for all lengths.

originality.rationale: Three accessible primary works were inspected at their definition, result and relevant bound sections. They introduce deletion-shadow optimization, maximal-run-limited VT intersections, and efficient RLL indel constructions, but their theorems do not give the sharp n=9 run-two capacity 13 or the first n=9 standard-VT restricted gap. Indexed related exact findings use different source restrictions or channels; historical priority remains qualified.
residual_risks: Unindexed historical code-size tables or supplementary material may already record the exact n=9 value and VT-class comparison.
The much earlier RLL coding literature, including Bours (1994), was identified through references but its full text was not inspected. It might contain a relevant finite table.
The bounded published-finding corpus semantic searches cannot establish exhaustive uniqueness, and the two closest indexed records use different constraints.

value.rationale: Run-ceiling-two binary coding is a natural constraint in storage and synchronization. Exact one-deletion capacity determines a concrete short-block payload limit, and the first n=9 failure of the standard VT-syndrome restriction exposes a structural optimality boundary: ordinary VT subclasses are optimal for all shorter allowed lengths but lose a whole codeword at nine. This is not a mere longer entry of an arbitrary table; its distinction is a motivated limitation of a classical construction. No general downstream theorem is claimed.
